The input already contains Chinese. Below is the English translation:

The judgment stated that the Alliance continued to publish its purposes, political stances, and ideology through its website, YouTube clips, and other channels. (File photo)

Website content: Linking the June 4th incident with the anti-extradition movement to rally protesters and amplify its voice

The judge held that from 1991 onwards, and even after the state amended the Constitution and the National Security Law took effect, the Alliance continued to adopt and promote the slogan "End one-party dictatorship" at its June 4th commemoration events; its actual words and deeds revealed the "essence" of its activities more than its articles of association.

The judgment pointed out that the Alliance's website, YouTube channel, and the "June 4th Memory · Human Rights Museum" website continuously published the Alliance's purposes, political stances, and ideology. The court considered most relevant to the case an online exhibition titled "Shared Fate, United in Struggle — 'The 1989 Democracy Movement and Hong Kong'," as well as an exhibition titled "Frontline Against Authoritarianism — From 'June 4th' to the Anti-Extradition Movement." The court held that the Alliance attempted to link June 4th with the social situation in Hong Kong at the time — "a concrete example of its attempt to rally or attract local protesters to join and amplify its voice."

The judge held that the Alliance's linking of June 4th with the anti-extradition movement was aimed at "instilling" in supporters the idea of ending one-party dictatorship and encouraging them to put it into practice. (File photo)

The judge pointed out that the "anti-extradition" events at the time were "well known" to involve not only criticism of the government but also large-scale unlawful protests. Given the social atmosphere at the time, the Alliance's "linking" of June 4th with the anti-extradition movement was aimed not only at "instilling" in supporters the idea of ending one-party dictatorship, but also at encouraging them to put it into practice.

The judgment also mentioned the June 4th Memory · Human Rights Museum website, stating that it preserved the memories of those involved in the June 4th incident, allowing people who had participated in commemoration events to revisit related content — including the message of "ending one-party dictatorship" — while those who had never participated could also receive the same textual information.

The judgment cited the Alliance's social media posts, including a speech by Szeto Wah in the Legislative Council in 2004. (File photo)

Facebook and Twitter: Expanding the reach of the Alliance's activities

The court pointed out that the Alliance used Facebook and Twitter (now X) to disseminate its messages at a wider and faster speed than through its website, amplifying the effectiveness of its physical activities. The judgment cited multiple posts, including a Facebook post dated 1 July 2020 titled "National Security Law — Trampling on Human Rights and the Rule of Law, Destroying One Country Two Systems," which read: "Facing the National Security Law, the #Alliance's position remains unchanged. We will continue to uphold the five major纲领 [major纲领], protest against one-party dictatorship, preserve the memory of June 4th, and support China's democracy movement. However, facing increasingly severe risks, we must also have contingency plans and prepare for prolonged struggle..."

The court held that this clearly demonstrated the Alliance continued to uphold "ending one-party dictatorship" after the National Security Law took effect, and anticipated that some supporters would put the slogan into practice — even if through non-violent means, this could still constitute "other unlawful means" under the National Security Law, hence the "increasingly severe risks" it faced.

Another Alliance post titled "Never Forget the June 4th Incident — Vindicate the 1989 Democracy Movement" quoted Szeto Wah's 2004 Legislative Council speech: "Chinese officials believe the Alliance must abandon the slogan of 'ending one-party dictatorship' before they will engage in dialogue with the democratic camp members participating in the Alliance... So-called 'dialogue' is merely wanting us to live forever under 'one-party dictatorship,' give up the pursuit of democracy and freedom, and be obedient citizens."

The court held that this post represented the consistent position of the Alliance and all defendants, and that reiterating this position after the National Security Law took effect was clearly intended to inform the public that it would, as always, uphold its stance and would not abandon its line of struggle in order to engage in dialogue with the central government. Given the Alliance's refusal to communicate with Beijing, the court did not accept that the standing committee members genuinely hoped to achieve "ending one-party dictatorship" through constitutional amendment.

The judge pointed out that the June 4th Memory · Human Rights Museum provided promotional materials printed with designs in the style of "Hongkongers, add oil," aimed at rallying social movement protesters to join and amplify its voice. (File photo)

June 4th Memory · Human Rights Museum: Promotional materials printed with the familiar social movement-style "Hongkongers, add oil" design

The judgment pointed out that the physical June 4th Memory · Human Rights Museum was open to the public, with the operating purpose of disseminating the Alliance's political stance to the public and serving as a venue for activities such as press conferences. The judge noted that the museum allowed the public to visit at a fixed location over the long term and thereby access information related to the Alliance and "ending one-party dictatorship," as evidenced by files on a USB flash drive seized by police.

The judge further pointed out that the promotional materials provided by the museum, apart from bearing the slogan "ending one-party dictatorship," were partly printed with the "Hongkongers, add oil" design commonly seen in Hong Kong social movement protests. The judge held that, beyond promoting "ending one-party dictatorship," the Alliance also hoped to rally or attract local social movement protesters to join and amplify its voice through its resistance-themed promotional materials.

The dissolved Alliance, as a legal entity, was listed as the first defendant in the case; the judge held that the Alliance could be prosecuted and, if convicted, punished. (File photo)

"Co-conspirator" statements

The court stated that in deciding whether to admit a co-conspirator's statements as evidence, it had considered the "co-conspirator rule" and accepted Chow Hang-tung's submission that if the speaker spoke in the capacity of the Alliance's chairman, vice-chairman, or standing committee member, such statements represented the Alliance's position. The judge noted that although the defendants disputed that some statements were made on behalf of the Alliance, this was not a decisive consideration, because the content did not materially diverge from the defendants' position.

The court stated that in applying the "attribution principle," it had carefully considered whether the words and deeds of the three defendants reflected the "dominant intent" of the Alliance, thereby allowing the court to regard the intentions and conduct deemed unlawful as those of the Alliance. After considering multiple statements made by some defendants in the presence of others in accordance with the "co-conspirator rule," the court ultimately found each defendant to be involved in a "joint criminal enterprise."
